raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old woman was referred to our hospital after having high fever and systemic joint pain for 10 days. She was admitted to our hospital for further examination and treatment. She had a past medical history of diabetes mellitus, herpes zoster, and lichen planus; her family history was unremarkable. On admission, her body temperature was 38.3 C, her blood pressure was 119/90 mmHg, her pulse rate was 110 beats/min, and the oxygen saturation in the room air was 97%. Erythematous papule appeared on the anterior chest and bilateral forearm. She had no pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, or abdominal pain. Her total white blood cell count was 9,200/microL (neutrophils 87%, lymphocytes 7%, and atypical lymphocytes 2%), CD4+ T cell was 44.3%, CD8+ T cell was 34.5%, hemoglobin was 15.3 g/dL, and platelet count was 123,000/microL. Her laboratory test results were as follows (Table 1): C-reactive protein level, 6.83 mg/dL; aspartate transaminase, 96 U/L; alanine transaminase, 130 U/L; alkaline phosphatase, 489 U/L; gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, 349 U/L; lactate dehydrogenase, 315 U/L; total bilirubin, 1.2 mg/dL; HbA1c, 8.7%; immunoglobulin G, 1574 mg/dL; immunoglobulin A, 186 mg/dL; immunoglobulin M, 144 mg/dL. The results of the serological tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. The result of renal function test was normal. Urinalysis showed negative occult blood and urinary protein. The blood cultures showed no growth. Because the patient continued to have high fever, we performed an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan, which revealed splenomegaly and a geographic low attenuation area in the dorsal and upper external side of the spleen (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)); this finding was consistent with splenic infarction.
We considered the splenic infarction to be in a hypercoagulable state. Her coagulopathy tests showed the following results: prothrombin time, 14.9 sec (normal, 10.6-14.9 sec); activated partial thromboplastin time, 33.9 sec (normal, 23.3-38.2 sec); d-dimer, 6.4 microg/mL; lupus anticoagulant, 1.05 (normal values <1.2, with dilute Russell's viper venom method); anticardiolipin antibody IgG, <8.0 U/mL; and anticardiolipin-beta2-glycoprotein I complex antibody, <1.2 U/mL. There were no abnormal coagulopathy results.
Because of atypical lymphocytosis and elevated transaminase, infectious mononucleosis was considered the cause of her sustained fever. The serological test for EBV antiviral capsid antigen IgM was negative at 0.1 (normal level, <0.5), antiviral capsid antigen IgG was positive at 7.5 (normal level, <0.5), and antibody to EBV nuclear antigen was positive at 4.6 (normal level, <0.5). These results suggest past infection for EBV. The serological test for CMV IgM was positive at 4.60 (normal level, <0.8), CMV IgG was slightly positive at 2.5 (normal level, <2.0), and parvovirus B19 IgM was also slightly positive at 0.99 (normal level, <0.8). The CMV antigen pp65 (antigenemia method of C10C11) was detectable at a level of 33 positive cells per 150,000 cells and 25 positive cells per 150,000 cells, which confirmed her diagnosis of acute CMV infection. The results of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) antigen/antibody and human T-cell leukemia virus type-1 (HTLV-1) antibody were negative. Although the patient was originally treated with conservative therapy, her fever persisted; therefore, she was subsequently treated with intravenous ganciclovir. The day after beginning the treatment with ganciclovir, her fever, joint pain, and erythematous papule improved (Figure 2). After 13 days of ganciclovir therapy, the CMV antigen pp65 was decreased at a level of 1 positive cells per 150,000 cells and she was discharged. Two weeks after the first serological tests of the virus antibodies, a follow-up serological test was performed. CMV IgM was positive at 4.80, CMV IgG was elevated to 11.7, and parvovirus B19 IgM was elevated to 2.38. Acute parvovirus infection was confirmed by the increasing level of parvovirus B19 IgM antibody. Seven weeks after discharge, we performed an additional abdominal CT scan. The splenic infarction area was decreased without atrophy, and splenomegaly was improved (Figures 1(c) and 1(d)).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of persistent high fever and systemic polyarthralgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred and admitted after experiencing 10 days of sustained high fever and generalized joint pain, accompanied on admission by erythematous papules on her anterior chest and bilateral forearms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.7%), prior herpes zoster, and lichen planus. Unremarkable family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 10 days of high fever, systemic joint pain, and anterior chest/forearm erythematous papules. Pertinent negatives: no pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, or abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.3 °C, blood pressure 119/90 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air; erythematous papular rash on the anterior chest and bilateral forearms; no pharyngitis, peripheral lymphadenopathy, or abdominal tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 9,200/uL (87% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes, 2% atypical lymphocytes; CD4+ T cells 44.3%, CD8+ T cells 34.5%), hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, mild thrombocytopenia with platelets 123,000/uL, CRP 6.83 mg/dL, AST 96 U/L, ALT 130 U/L, ALP 489 U/L, GGT 349 U/L, LDH 315 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, HbA1c 8.7%, IgG 1,574 mg/dL, IgA 186 mg/dL, IgM 144 mg/dL, normal renal function, and negative urinalysis and blood cultures. Coagulation/thrombophilia panel: PT 14.9 s (normal 10.6-14.9 s), aPTT 33.9 s (normal 23.3-38.2 s), elevated D-dimer 6.4 ug/mL, normal lupus anticoagulant (dRVVT 1.05, normal <1.2), anticardiolipin IgG <8.0 U/mL, and anti-cardiolipin-beta2-GPI complex <1.2 U/mL. Viral serologies: HBV, HCV, HIV-1 Ag/Ab, and HTLV-1 negative; EBV VCA-IgM negative (0.1), VCA-IgG positive (7.5), and EBNA positive (4.6) indicating past EBV infection; CMV IgM positive at 4.60 (normal <0.8; 4.80 at 2 weeks), CMV IgG weakly positive at 2.5 (normal <2.0; rising to 11.7 at 2 weeks), and parvovirus B19 IgM weakly positive at 0.99 (normal <0.8; rising to 2.38 at 2 weeks).
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed splenomegaly and a wedge-shaped geographic low-attenuation splenic infarction in the dorsal/superior-lateral spleen (which decreased in size without atrophy alongside improved splenomegaly on 7-week post-discharge follow-up CT). Peripheral blood CMV pp65 antigenemia (C10/C11 method) was positive at 33 and 25 positive cells per 150,000 WBCs (decreasing to 1 positive cell per 150,000 WBCs after 13 days of IV ganciclovir).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of acute primary cytomegalovirus (CMV) and human parvovirus B19 co-infection complicated by atraumatic splenic infarction in a non-anticoagulated diabetic woman, confirmed by positive CMV pp65 antigenemia (33 and 25 positive cells/150,000 WBCs), CMV IgM positivity (4.60 to 4.80) with CMV IgG seroconversion (2.5 to 11.7), and rising parvovirus B19 IgM titers (0.99 to 2.38), with antiphospholipid antibodies excluded. After persistent fever on initial conservative management, treatment with intravenous ganciclovir for 13 days produced rapid improvement in fever, polyarthralgia, and rash within 24 hours, reduction of CMV pp65 antigenemia to 1/150,000 cells at discharge, and regression of the splenic infarction on 7-week follow-up CT.
